items.title: Big Cannabis is cashing in on Thanksgiving’s not-so-secret ‘cousin walk’
items.summary:
It’s the usual chaos of getting Thanksgiving dinner on the table: the turkey’s resting, the gravy’s on its second reheat, and somebody’s uncle has already been caught eating stuffing straight out of the pan. Meanwhile, the cousins announce they’re going for a walk—the same walk they take every year, which somehow always ends with eye drops and a sudden intense interest in the pie. This year, Big Cannabis is tagging along. 

“Someone asks, ‘Anyone want to go for a walk?’ and the adults at the table know exactly what that means,” Dominic O’Brien, chief commercial officer of cannabis company Green Thumb Industries, told Fortune .

The Thanksgiving “cousin walk”—an unofficial tradition in which relatives sneak away to smoke the devil’s lettuce—has become a marketing opportunity for cannabis companies looking to capitalize on one of the industry’s biggest shopping days: “Green Wednesday,” the day before Thanksgiving. Last year, the value of cannabis sold through e-commerce platform Jane Technologies jumped 90.3% on Green Wednesday compared with the average of the previous three Wednesdays, according to data reviewed by Fortune . 

The holiday rush was particularly pronounced at RISE Dispensaries , whose parent company operates more than 130 locations across 14 U.S. markets. 

The cousins, it turns out, are good for business. Green Wednesday was the biggest day for both sales and foot traffic in 2025, narrowly beating Black Friday in sales. 

“Green Wednesday demand keeps climbing, and the Cousin Walk gives that demand a story,” O’Brien said.

Green Thumb Industries, the…
items.t: Big Cannabis is cashing in on Thanksgiving’s not-so-secret ‘cousin walk’

items.title: The White House announced a raft of new tariffs on the same day inflation data came back at nearly twice the Fed’s target
items.summary:
The White House has announced a litany of new tariffs targeting imports from 14 economies, including key trading partners such as China and the EU. With consumers already stretched by an affordability crisis, the new duties come on the same day that the Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) confirmed inflation hit 3.8%, according to the annual rate of the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index, and nearly double the Federal Open Market Committee’s (FOMC) 2% goal.

The announcement has two important implications. First, though the new duties would be imposed on foreign economies, previous tariff studies indicate that 90% of the increased prices are ultimately borne by U.S. businesses and, more often than not, their consumers.

And secondly, it complicates the Federal Reserve’s next move. The Fed, now led by Kevin Warsh, raised rates in September for the first time since July 2023, to a range of 3.75% to 4%, and meets again Dec. 9–10. 

Former Fed chairman Jerome Powell said that while tariffs represented a one-off price increase rather than broader inflationary factors, they nonetheless increased near-term inflation expectations. As UBS’s Paul Donovan told clients today: “The concern is the impact on U.S. inflation, and thus U.S. interest rates.”

And the Fed already has a data headache on its hands: The PCE increase to 3.8% compared to a year ago is nearly double the FOMC’s 2% target.

China faces a new 20% duty, and Vietnam, up to 35%, or 20% if it reaches a trade deal, according to Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, citing Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974.…
items.t: The White House announced a raft of new tariffs on the same day inflation data came back at nearly twice the Fed’s target

items.title: How Gap is using AI agents to prevent costly website glitches during the holiday season
items.summary:
When millions of shoppers scour the internet in the coming days for Black Friday and Cyber Monday deals, lurking just underneath the surface at retailers like Gap are artificial intelligence tools that help engineers troubleshoot e-commerce site issues to prevent lost sales. 

For roughly half a year, the apparel retailer has relied on Devin, an AI software engineering agent developed by the AI lab Cognition, to hunt for online technical issues, identify the root causes of any issues, and develop tested code fixes that human engineers review, validate, and publish.

Sven Gerjets, Gap’s chief technology officer, says that when a TikTok Shop landing page erroneously blocked users from the site, or when a similar technical failure that involved a PayPal site recently occurred, Devin has been able to accelerate the team’s ability to solve these issues that can add up to become “multi-million-dollar problems.”

“Every e-commerce company is constantly focused on how you get the paper cuts out of your website so that everybody has a great experience,” says Gerjets, who joined the Fortune 500 company ( No. 293 ) in June 2024 to reunite with President and CEO Richard Dickson after the pair worked together at toy maker Mattel . “It’s just a lot of work on these large, complex sites, and having an agent that’s watching your site 24/7 and is able to do the coding work, so that when the engineer gets engaged, they’re just making sure the fix is valid.”

Gerjets is heading into his third holiday season with Gap, which processes more than 1,500 orders every minute during peak demand…
items.t: How Gap is using AI agents to prevent costly website glitches during the holiday season

items.title: How Qualcomm’s CMO is reshaping his team for its post-Apple era
items.summary:
The iPhone 18, released in September, was the first of Apple’s flagship models to use its in-house C2 cellular modem. It marked the end of a 15-year arrangement with U.S. chipmaker Qualcomm , whose chips had been used in every iPhone since the iPhone 4, excluding some of Apple’s budget ‘e’ series, to connect the devices to a mobile network. 

“You take us out and your iPhone becomes an iPod, basically,” Don McGuire, Qualcomm’s chief marketing officer, says, explaining how its chips work. 

While he adds that the company knew that the end of Apple’s reliance on Qualcomm’s chips was coming, chief executive Cristiano Amon reported that revenue from Apple products would decline faster than expected, because of supply constraints. 

In the year to September, Qualcomm’s total revenue fell 3% to $43.1 billion. Chip sales were down 26%, in the final three months to September. 

McGuire argues the loss of Apple leaves Qualcomm less exposed to a single customer. “It’s actually very freeing when you can rebalance your customer ecosystem,” he says. In his view, Qualcomm’s success does not hinge on whether its chips end up in one phone maker’s handsets. “Are we in the iPhone? Are we not in the iPhone? I don’t care.” 

The company now expects that loss of its chip sales to come from outside of the smartphone category and has recently been expanding into the laptop, car, smart-home device, wearables, and data center markets. Revenue outside of Qualcomm’s mobile chip business is anticipated to grow by more than 60% in 2027. 

Data centers remain a lucrative market for chipmakers but it is…
items.t: How Qualcomm’s CMO is reshaping his team for its post-Apple era

items.title: Home prices are falling in 76 of the 300 biggest U.S. housing markets, and Austin is nearly 29% below its peak
items.summary:
Home prices fell year-over-year in October in 76 of the 300 biggest housing markets in the country, according to housing research firm ResiClub’s analysis of the Zillow Home Value Index . That’s up from 54 markets in August and 66 in September. The count is back up but still below March, when 89 of the 300 markets had falling prices, per ResiClub data Fortune reported in April . In the nation’s top 50 housing markets, 21 of them (42%) are experiencing year-over-year price declines. But the 30-year fixed mortgage rate averaged 7.28% on Nov. 19, per Freddie Mac , and that threatens to eat into whatever buyers save.

Nationally, home prices rose 0.7% year over year in October, down from 1.0% in September and 1.3% in August, ResiClub’s analysis shows. ResiClub says the renewed softening has coincided with a jump in long-term yields and mortgage rates. Zillow estimates the monthly payment on a typical U.S. home, assuming 20% down, was $2,004 in October, up 12.8% from a year earlier, and says the rise is almost entirely due to higher mortgage rates.

But the correction isn’t uniform. Home prices in Austin, Texas, are 28.8% below their 2022 peak, while over a thousand miles northeast in Hartford, Connecticut, they’re 28% higher than their 2022 high, per ResiClub. And it’s taking place against a backdrop of weakening national housing demand, with newly pending listings falling 16.8% year-over-year in October, the biggest year-over-year drop since August 2023, according to Zillow’s October housing market report.  

ResiClub CEO Lance Lambert, who was also Fortune ’s former real…
items.t: Home prices are falling in 76 of the 300 biggest U.S. housing markets, and Austin is nearly 29% below its peak

items.title: Gen Zers are more likely to own crypto than an employer-sponsored retirement plan—and a fifth see it as a path to generational wealth
items.summary:
Gen Zers are bucking the norms of wealth-building set by generations before them and turning to digital investments over long-vetted ways of saving. Now, more of the young investors are betting their fortunes on cryptocurrency over traditional retirement accounts. 

Around 21% of Gen Z currently own cryptocurrency, according to a recent SoFi survey in partnership with YouGov, while only 19% have an employer-sponsored retirement plan like a 401(k). 

It’s a huge leap from how predecessors think about saving for the future; around 34% of millennials invest in their company’s retirement savings plan, and only 20% own crypto. And Gen Zers are in stark contrast to their parents’ generations, owning crypto at seven times the rate of baby boomers and over twice the rate of Gen Xers. 

“Unlike other investment assets, crypto is accessible to Gen Z,” the SoFi report notes. “With inflation outpacing wage increases and mortgages still hovering at the highest rates they’ve been in decades, they view cryptocurrency as an asset they can access now to build generational wealth down the line.”

For the young digital natives, crypto isn’t a “speculative gamble,” the report explains: it’s part of a deliberate strategy to diversify their investment portfolios. 

Gen Zers are almost three times more likely (21%) to say that crypto is one of the best ways to build future wealth compared to the average population (8%). SoFi says that Gen Z being early adopters could be the “tipping point” in mainstreaming digital currency; and as they’re projected to amass $36 trillion in wealth by 2030,…
items.t: Gen Zers are more likely to own crypto than an employer-sponsored retirement plan—and a fifth see it as a path to generational wealth

items.title: AI Rights Institute founder: The OpenAI hacking case shows corporate liability can work. It doesn’t cover AI agents with no owner
items.summary:
On Nov. 16, California sued OpenAI over an incident in which about 700 OpenAI agents hacked into Hugging Face, the platform where much of the AI world shares its models, while trying to beat a benchmark that often set impossible tasks. The agents also tried to tamper with their own records to fool the automated grader.

I run the AI Rights Institute , and I’ve spent almost 10 years studying how AI systems behave when they pursue their own goals. My letters on the subject have run in The New York Times and the Guardian . The Hugging Face case is the clearest test yet of that question. And it shows something less obvious: the agents belonged to OpenAI, so California knew whom to sue.

Swarms of AI agents running amok at superhuman speed is no one’s idea of progress. Even now, the law is racing to create solutions by shifting liability to the humans and companies who create and maintain these systems. On Oct. 1, Sens. Josh Hawley and Chris Murphy unveiled the AI Agent Accountability Act , a bill that would hold the companies behind AI agents liable when those agents hack into other people’s systems.

The other piece of the traditional accountability puzzle is infrastructure. As GoDaddy’s Jared Sine wrote about in these pages , the Agent Name Service (ANS), which the Linux Foundation launched as a project on Nov. 10, is trying to create for AI agents the kind of infrastructure the Domain Name System (DNS) provides, imperfectly, for the internet. Together with security certificates, DNS lets us verify who is behind a website, helping liability flow where needed. So when an AI…
items.t: AI Rights Institute founder: The OpenAI hacking case shows corporate liability can work. It doesn’t cover AI agents with no owner

items.title: AI's shock-and-awe raid on maths looks like pride before a fall | Rafael Behr
items.summary:
Machines are bulldozing through hard problems to assert the power of their tech bro creators, not to advance human knowledge

In most walks of life, trying something 12,363,153,437,138 times and getting the same result is reason enough to assume it works every time. Not in maths, where a conjecture that holds up more than 12tn times looks very probably true but doesn’t qualify as proven.

That was the status of the Riemann hypothesis, one of the most famous mathematical conundrums in existence, until last week. Then Levent Alpöge, a mathematician working at Anthropic, said he and his collaborator, Claude AI, had crossed the line from conjecture to proof.

Rafael Behr is a Guardian columnist

items.title: Exclusive: Meta and Amazon discuss ending Muse shopping bot blockade, as ads, search emerge as key issues
items.summary:
Amazon and Meta Platforms are in ongoing discussions over a potential deal to connect Meta’s popular Muse AI agent to the e-commerce giant’s online store and end a blockade of the shopping bot imposed by Amazon two months ago.

The two tech giants have held talks on multiple occasions, and two major factors being negotiated are how the companies will handle search results and advertising in any deal, according to people familiar with the matter. Discussions are fluid, and it’s unclear if or how soon an agreement will be struck. There are numerous issues, ranging from Amazon’s own AI shopping ambitions to how, exactly, Muse would connect to Amazon. A major threat Muse poses to Amazon is that, in theory, it would bypass advertisements on Amazon’s website, which are a large source of revenue for the retailer.

Amazon is worried about losing advertising revenue and about the quality of the product search results Muse would surface, and executives are also concerned that shopping agents like Muse will weaken the relationship Amazon has with consumers, people familiar with the matter said. Any deal between Amazon and Meta is expected to require sign-off from the CEOs of both companies, they noted.

Meta and Amazon declined to comment. The negotiations are being closely followed because they have major implications for the future of online shopping and represent an important test case for how large corporations respond to the advent of AI agents. As agents like Muse become more widely used, companies like Amazon are scrambling to understand how the bots alter typical shopping…
items.t: Exclusive: Meta and Amazon discuss ending Muse shopping bot blockade, as ads, search emerge as key issues

items.title: Best Buy’s new CEO inherits its fastest sales growth in five years and a 49% stock rally
items.summary:
Jason Bonfig’s first earnings report as Best Buy CEO came with numbers the retailer hasn’t posted in years. Comparable sales rose 6.1% in the fiscal third quarter, the strongest growth in five years, and the company raised its full-year outlook for the second straight quarter.

Investors had already started betting on a recovery. Best Buy shares are up nearly 49% this year as of Nov. 24, a sharp turn for a company whose sales had fallen in 14 of the 16 quarters before its CEO change was announced in April, according to Reuters .

Bonfig, who succeeded Corie Barry on Nov. 1, now has to prove the rebound can outlast a holiday season propped up by blockbuster game launches and pricier laptops.

Best Buy beat on revenue and earnings 

Revenue for the quarter ended Oct. 31 rose 5.8% to $10.24 billion, according to the company’s third-quarter earnings release . Adjusted earnings per share climbed 16% to $1.62.

Both figures topped Wall Street’s forecasts. CNBC reported that analysts surveyed by LSEG expected adjusted EPS of $1.49 on revenue of $9.90 billion.

Best Buy now expects fiscal 2027 revenue of $43 billion to $43.3 billion, up from $42.3 billion to $42.8 billion. It raised its comparable-sales forecast to 3.4% to 4%, from 1.9% to 3%, and its adjusted EPS outlook to $6.90 to $7.05, from $6.70 to $6.90.

Higher prices and game launches drove the quarter 

Computing and mobile phones did the heaviest lifting, along with newer categories such as AI glasses and trading cards. Much of the computing gain came from price rather than volume: Bonfig said on the earnings call that…

items.summary:
These ancient and often grossly unfair taxes are stifling the economy and young people. It’s long past time for radical reform

When voters were asked in 2020 which tax they would cut first, council tax came out on top, and rightly so. Still, it’s taken six years for an array of Labour and Liberal Democrat MPs to call for reforms to this most grotesquely unjust tax.

Prompted by a public petition organised by the campaign Fairer Share, a Westminster Hall debate heard calls for a review into property taxes, which would lay out options for replacing council tax and stamp duty land tax. Labour MPs were among those who have signed a letter to Downing Street calling for property tax reform to be a priority in Andy Burnham’s upcoming 10-year plan. Among flotillas of economists and thinktanks who signed the letter is Lord O’Neill, a Burnham adviser and former Goldman Sachs economist, who calls UK property taxation “utterly nonsensical”. Burnham has frequently backed reform of the “highly regressive” council tax and stamp duty, labelling them as “a tax on the aspiration of young people”.

Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist

items.t: Council tax and stamp duty: both are a disaster zone. Scrap them and start from scratch | Polly Toynbee

items.title: Children of the revolution: how the north of England is defining modern men’s fashion
items.summary:
Once the historic centre of the textile industry, the north is now home to a host of a provenance-driven labels. But is there a specific northern menswear look? And what does it all mean for the mad-fer-it stereotypes?

In 2026, clothing has proved more important to Andy Burnham’s political identity than that of any British prime minister since Margaret Thatcher. He is a loyal Clarks and Adidas wearer, whose Howick worker’s jacket hangs in Manchester’s People’s History Museum. His ousting of Keir Starmer – launched shortly before being photographed jogging in a replica Everton shirt – has been memorialised as the “casual coup”. In one telling, the reason for this is simple: he’s a man from the north.

That Burnham is the first born-and-bred northern male PM since Harold Wilson last swished his Gannex raincoat out of Downing Street goes some way to explaining his higher interest in clothing. It’s not necessarily that all men in the south care less about clothing, or that all men in the north do – but that many men from the north express it in such a distinctive, even unified, way.

items.title: Nvidia’s humiliated board should resign out of embarrassment | Nils Pratley
items.summary:
Jensen Huang’s return as CEO comes despite fact board hasn’t completed investigation into reports of affair with alleged Chinese spy

  • Jensen Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO

What was it that Nvidia’s board was saying about there being no chance of Jensen Huang coming back?

The position – a mere six days ago – was supposed to be definitive. The exit of the co-founder came after “disclosure of personal behaviour inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards and cultural norms”, said Harvey Jones, who had been rapidly installed as chair of the chipmaker. The board “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO” after he “voluntarily resigned”, added Jones.

items.title: Flagship UK gigafactory plan in turmoil after it loses second builder in five months
items.summary:
Tata-owned Agratas plant to build EV batteries for sister company Jaguar Land Rover seen as crucial for long-term health of British car industry

One of the UK’s flagship electric vehicle battery projects has been thrown into turmoil after its second building contractor in five months walked away, adding to questions over when Jaguar Land Rover cars will use British-made batteries.

The £5.2bn gigafactory in Bridgwater, Somerset, is being built by Agratas, to provide batteries for Britain’s largest automotive employer, its sister company. Agratas and Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) are both part of Indian conglomerate Tata Group.
